extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / voters and citizens considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative guidance for assessing and defending the proposed federal Constitution during the ratification debate, addressing objections about bills of rights, trial by jury, remoteness, expense, and the general powers of the national government. The text sets out standards by which the constitutionality, sufficiency, and prudence of provisions should be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury protection in criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The security of liberty is materially concerned only in the trial by jury in criminal cases, which is provided for in the most ample manner in the plan of the convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that constitutional protection of jury trial for criminal offenses is essential; this is the primary sphere where the institution secures liberty. Less insistence is required for civil cases, which may remain under state constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional establishment of jury in all cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of the trial by jury in ALL cases would have been an unpardonable error in the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not enshrine jury trial for every conceivable case in the national constitution; such blanket provisions would be unprecedented and could prove impractical or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to legislatures for evolving procedural limits
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible in the nature of the thing to fix the salutary point at which the operation of the institution ought to stop, and this is ... a strong argument for leaving the matter to the discretion of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer flexible legislative authority over rigid constitutional prescriptions for procedural institutions whose appropriate scope may shift with social change and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of adopting one State's institutions as national standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Massachusetts proposition ... cannot operate as a general regulation, until some uniform plan ... shall be adopted by the different States. ... it is not very probable the other States would entertain the same opinion of our institutions as we do ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing national constitutional rules on any single State's institutions because diversity of state systems and state pride will make such a model unacceptable or unworkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of rights are unnecessary in a government founded on the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of rights ... have no application to constitutions professedly founded upon the power of the people, and executed by their immediate representatives and servants. Here, in strictness, the people surrender nothing; and as they retain every thing they have no need of particular reservations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sovereignty originates with the people, a separate bill of rights may be redundant; the structure of government itself can embody protections of liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of rights can be dangerous by implying constructive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: They would contain various exceptions to powers not granted; and, on this very account, would afford a colorable pretext to claim more than were granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that enumerating prohibitions or rights might create interpretive openings (constructive powers) that enable claims of additional national authority; sometimes omission avoids unintended implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial constitutional provisions constitute a bill of rights by substance, not form
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution, if adopted, will be the bill of rights of the Union. ... Adverting therefore to the substantial meaning of a bill of rights, it is absurd to allege that it is not to be found in the work of the convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether protections exist in substance (habeas corpus, prohibitions on ex post facto laws, trial by jury, etc.), regardless of whether labelled a 'bill of rights'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in cases of rebellion or invasion the public safety may require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat an explicit constitutional guarantee of habeas corpus as a core security against arbitrary imprisonment and an important constitutional safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of bills of attainder and ex post facto laws
rubrics_metrics.description: No bill of attainder or ex-post-facto law shall be passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count express constitutional bans on legislative punishments and retroactive criminal laws as significant protections of individual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: No title of nobility shall be granted by the United States; and no person holding any office of profit or trust under them, shall, without the consent of the Congress, accept of any present, emolument, office, or title of any kind whatever, from any king, prince, or foreign state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit bar on nobility is a foundational republican safeguard and should be valued as such when assessing the constitution's protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal trial venue and jury rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial of all crimes, except in cases of impeachment, shall be by jury; and such trial shall be held in the State where the said crimes shall have been committed; but when not committed within any State, the trial shall be at such place or places as the Congress may by law have directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the constitution secures jury trials and sensible venue rules for criminal prosecutions; these details are central to criminal justice protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treason defined and conviction standard narrowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Treason against the United States shall consist only in levying war against them, or in adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort. No person shall be convicted of treason, unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or on confession in open court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to narrow definitions of capital or high crimes (like treason) and high evidentiary standards as protections against political abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited consequences of impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than to removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States; but the party convicted shall, nevertheless, be liable and subject to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment according to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider explicit constitutional limits on impeachment penalties as safeguards of legal fairness and separation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on public opinion and civic spirit for certain liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the liberty of the press? ... its security, whatever fine declarations may be inserted in any constitution respecting it, must altogether depend on public opinion, and on the general spirit of the people and of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some liberties (e.g., freedom of the press) ultimately rest on culture, public opinion, and institutional practice as much as on textual guarantees; assess both legal text and social context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake formal declarations for effective protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The only use of the declaration was to recognize the ancient law and to remove doubts... This consequently can be considered as no part of a declaration of rights, which under our constitutions must be intended as limitations of the power of the government itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether declaratory clauses truly limit governmental power or merely acknowledge existing law; substantive limitations are more important than ornamental statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing remoteness of national government and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in most of the arguments which relate to distance a palpable illusion of the imagination. ... The executive and legislative bodies of each State will be so many sentinels over the persons employed in every department of the national administration; and ... they can never be at a loss to know the behavior of those who represent their constituents in the national councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging objections that the national seat is too remote, consider channels of information (public prints, correspondence), the role of state governments as monitors, and the ability of citizens to obtain knowledge of national representatives' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expense of national government vs. savings and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of additional expense from the establishment of the proposed Constitution are much fewer than may have been imagined; that they are counterbalanced by considerable objects of saving; ... the sessions of the State legislatures will be protracted greatly beyond what was necessary... The difference ... will alone form an article of saving...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate projected increases in public expense against anticipated savings (reduced duplication of effort, shorter sessions, substitution of state for federal officers) and the increased efficiency of a national executive handling many tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as security against local faction, foreign intrigue, and military dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional securities ... consist chiefly in the restraints which the preservation of the Union will impose on local factions and insurrections, ... in the diminution of the opportunities to foreign intrigue, ... in the prevention of extensive military establishments, ... in the express guaranty of a republican form of government to each; in the absolute and universal exclusion of titles of nobility; and in the precautions against the repetition of those practices on the part of the State governments which have undermined the foundations of property and credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a constitution by its capacity to protect republican government, property, and national safety through structural means (union, guarantees, prohibitions) and its ability to restrain destructive local or foreign influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance and practical operation over verbal/formal distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of what has been said on this subject rests merely on verbal and nominal distinctions, entirely foreign from the substance of the thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating constitutional adequacy, focus on practical effects and substantive safeguards rather than formal labels or rhetorical distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for adaptability to changing social circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The changes which are continually happening in the affairs of society may render a different mode of determining questions of property preferable in many cases in which that mode of trial now prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional norms to permit future legislative or institutional adaptation where necessary; avoid over-rigid constitutional prescriptions that foreclose improvement.
